# swarmops update

Replace this program, swarmops and so, with the latest release, or set automatic update. Touches no store and never runs upgrade.

Without a flag it reads the latest release from where GitHub's releases page redirects, and when that is newer than what is installed it downloads the release, checks it against the release's SHA256SUMS, runs the new binaries once, and renames them over the old ones, swarmops first: updated is true and previous is the version replaced. A latest release that is not newer installs nothing and is no error; an older version or a pre-release is never installed. Running MCP servers keep the program they started with until they are restarted.

It works on an install the installer made, which left a receipt beside the binaries (.swarmops-receipt), in a release's build. Any other install is refused as E\_INVALID\_ARG, details.reason no\_receipt or not\_a\_release\_build, and is updated the way it was installed: by its package, or by building again. Nothing that turns automatic update off stops this command.

It runs the host's curl for the one request of its own (SWARMOPS\_CURL by an absolute path, else the first on PATH; none is details.reason curl\_missing), and the installer built into this program, under /bin/sh, with the tools that needs: curl or wget, tar, and sha256sum or shasum. One update runs at a time for an install: a second is E\_BUSY, details.reason update\_running. A host that does not answer is E\_REMOTE\_UNREACHABLE, details.phase update. A download, check or replacement that fails is E\_IO with details.step (install, verify, swap, lock or receipt): before the two renames nothing was replaced.

--auto off and --auto on write the receipt's auto\_update, and --status says whether the install updates itself (auto\_update: on, or what turned it off) and gives the note a run in the background left (pending). SWARMOPS\_AUTO\_UPDATE=off turns automatic update off for the processes that have it; CI and a container turn it off unless that variable is on; root's install, and one in another user's directory, never update themselves. --background does what automatic update does: with automatic update on, it installs the latest release only when that carries the mark for the installed minor line (auto-update-from-&lt;major&gt;.&lt;minor&gt;, a file of the release), and leaves a note beside the binaries; a release without the mark is noted at its second sighting, and a request that fails changes nothing and is no error.

Where automatic update is on, a command that went well starts update --background once a day, after its envelope is out, and waits for nothing: its output and exit code do not change. The next such command whose stderr is a terminal prints the note, one line on stderr after its envelope, once. mcp, serve, auth git-credential, ws hook and update itself start no such run and print no note.

```yaml
title: "swarmops update"
description: "Replace this program, swarmops and so, with the latest release, or set automatic update. Touches no store and never runs upgrade."
group: "store"
since: "0.12.0"
mutates: false
identity_required: false
mcp_tool: ""
envelope_op: "update"
exit_codes: [0, 2]
errors: [E_INVALID_ARG]
syntax: "swarmops update [OPTIONS]"
```

## Syntax

```text
swarmops update [OPTIONS]
```

## Required arguments

None.

## Optional arguments

The command also takes the [global options](../cli.md#global-options).

### `--check`

Syntax: `--check`.

Look for the latest release and say what it is: install nothing.

### `--auto`

Syntax: `--auto <SWITCH>`.

Turn this install's automatic update on or off, in its receipt. Reaches no network. Values: `on`: Automatic update on; `off`: Automatic update off.

### `--status`

Syntax: `--status`.

Say whether this install updates itself, and what decided so. Reaches no network.

### `--background`

Syntax: `--background`.

Do what automatic update does: install the latest release only if it is marked for the installed line, and leave a note of what was done.

## Examples

### CLI

```sh
swarmops update --status
```

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "op": "update",
  "api": 1,
  "result": {
    "current": "[version]",
    "updated": false,
    "auto_update": "off_source_build"
  },
  "meta": {
    "elapsed_ms": "[elapsed_ms]",
    "resolved": {},
    "auth": "trust"
  }
}
```

Exit code 0. Recorded by the CLI tests. A name in square brackets, such as `[tmp]` or `[c1]`, stands for what differs from run to run: the test's temporary directory, an id, a time.

## Details

`update` replaces the program itself, `swarmops` and `so`, with the latest release, and holds the
switch of automatic update. It opens no store: `--repo` and `--as` are read and not used, and
the envelope has no `meta.repo`. It never changes a store, and never runs
[`upgrade`](../commands/upgrade.md), which is the store's command and yours alone to run. It
has no MCP tool: a call would replace the program the server runs from.

The forms are one at a time: no flag installs, `--check` looks, `--auto on|off` and `--status`
are the switch ([Automatic update's switch](#automatic-updates-switch)), and `--background` is
what automatic update runs ([In the background](#in-the-background)) after a command
([After a command](#after-a-command)).

### What it updates

Only an install the installer made, in a build a release holds:

| The binaries came from | `update` |
| --- | --- |
| The installer (`install.sh`) | Works. The installer leaves a receipt beside them, `.swarmops-receipt`. |
| A `.deb` or `.rpm`, or a server image | `E_INVALID_ARG`, `details.reason` `no_receipt`, with `details.dir`. Install the next release's package. |
| An archive unpacked by hand, or an installer older than the receipt | `no_receipt`. Running the installer once, with `--dir` naming the directory, leaves a receipt. |
| A clone (`cargo install`, `cargo build`) | `not_a_release_build`, whatever is beside them. Build the newer source. |

The install is the directory the running program's own file is in, with every link on the way
followed: `so` reached through a link in another directory updates the directory it points
into. A release's build that cannot find its own file is `E_INVALID_ARG` (`details.reason`
`exe_unknown`). A file by the receipt's name that is no receipt (not TOML, without
`receipt = 1`, without `auto_update = true` or `false`, or over 64 KiB) is refused by every
form (`details.reason` `receipt`, `details.path`) and never written over.

### What an update does

1. **The latest release.** One HEAD request to
   `https://github.com/KeiaiLab/SwarmOps/releases/latest`, which GitHub answers with a redirect
   to the latest release's page. The redirect is not followed. Its address must be exactly
   `https://github.com/KeiaiLab/SwarmOps/releases/tag/v<X.Y.Z>`, three plain numbers: anything
   else, a pre-release's page among it, is `E_REMOTE_UNREACHABLE`. GitHub's `latest` never
   names a pre-release.
2. **What is installed.** `swarmops --version` and `so --version` in the install directory; the
   lower of the two counts, so that an update stopped between the two names is finished by the
   next one. A name that is missing, or answers as another program, has no version, and then
   the install has none: `current` is the running program's own.
3. **Only a newer release.** A latest release that is not strictly newer installs nothing:
   `updated` is `false`, exit 0. A pre-release is older than its release. Nothing ever installs
   a version older than the program that runs, whatever the two names answer: GitHub's `latest`
   can name an older release, after one was deleted or when a patch of an older line was
   published last. To go back, or to pin a version, run the installer with `--version`, which
   also turns automatic update off. Where the install has no version, a latest release that is
   the running program's own version or a newer one is installed, and writes both names, as
   the installer does: a program of your own named `so` in that directory is replaced. Only
   an `update` you run does that; the run in the background installs nothing there.
4. **Download, check, unpack.** The installer built into the program runs under `/bin/sh` for
   that release, into `.swarmops-update.d` beside the binaries: it downloads the archive for
   this host and the release's `SHA256SUMS`, checks the one against the other, and unpacks the
   two binaries. It is the installer this build's source holds, not one fetched for the
   occasion, and it refuses what the installer refuses: a host without a build in the release,
   a glibc older than the release needs, a checksum that does not match.
5. **Run before replacing.** Each staged binary is run once and must print exactly
   `swarmops <X.Y.Z>`, the release's line. One that does not start on this host, or is another
   version, replaces nothing.
6. **Replace.** The staged `swarmops` is renamed over the installed one, then `so`, and the
   directory is flushed. Each name is whole at every moment. Between the two renames `swarmops`
   is new and `so` old; step 2 repairs an update that stopped there.

`previous` is the version replaced and `current` the one installed when the command ended;
`latest` and `notes` are the latest release and its page. A process that already runs keeps the
program it started with: a `swarmops mcp` server serves with the old one until it is restarted.

One update runs at a time for an install. A second `update` is `E_BUSY` (`details.reason`
`update_running`, exit 4): run it again when the first has ended. The lock is
`.swarmops-update.lock` beside the binaries, held from before the latest release is asked for
until the binaries are replaced, and freed by the system however the process ends. The installer
itself takes no lock: do not run it into the same directory while an update runs.

### What it runs, and what that sends

SwarmOps has no network code of its own.

- **curl, for the latest release.** One run of the curl `SWARMOPS_CURL` names by an absolute
  path, else the first `curl` on `PATH`, as [`auth login`](../commands/auth-login.md) runs
  it: the request on its stdin, a cleared environment but for `PATH`, the proxy variables and
  the certificate variables, https only, TLS 1.2 or later, no redirect followed. A host without
  curl is `E_INVALID_ARG` (`details.reason` `curl_missing`), also where the installer itself
  would have used wget. The request carries no token; GitHub sees your address, the
  repository's path, and the header `User-Agent: swarmops-update`, which names no version.
- **The installer, for the release.** `/bin/sh` and the tools the installer needs on `PATH`:
  curl or wget, tar, and sha256sum or shasum. It gets `PATH`, `HOME`, `TMPDIR`, the proxy
  variables and the certificate variables, and no other variable: `SWARMOPS_VERSION`,
  `SWARMOPS_INSTALL_DIR` and the installer's test seams do not reach it. It downloads from
  `https://github.com/KeiaiLab/SwarmOps/releases/download/`, following GitHub's redirects, with
  its downloader's own headers. What it prints is read and dropped; its last line is in the
  error when it fails. It is stopped after ten minutes.

What this is checked against: HTTPS to GitHub, and the release's own `SHA256SUMS`, which comes
from the same place as the archive. No signature is checked, as none is by the installer. A
release older than what is installed is never taken, so an old release cannot be replayed; a
host that is shown no newer release at all cannot tell. These requests have been tested against
stand-ins on the testing host, and not yet run against GitHub.

### What can fail

| What happened | Error | `details` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The build is no release's | `E_INVALID_ARG` | `reason` `not_a_release_build` |
| No receipt is beside the binaries | `E_INVALID_ARG` | `reason` `no_receipt`, `dir` |
| The receipt is none this build reads | `E_INVALID_ARG` | `reason` `receipt`, `path` |
| The program cannot find its own file | `E_INVALID_ARG` | `reason` `exe_unknown` |
| There is no curl | `E_INVALID_ARG` | `reason` `curl_missing` |
| Another update runs | `E_BUSY` | `reason` `update_running` |
| curl reached no answer | `E_REMOTE_UNREACHABLE` | `phase` `update`, `host`, `cause`, `curl_exit` |
| The answer names no release | `E_REMOTE_UNREACHABLE` | `phase` `update`, `host`, `http_status` when it had one |
| The lock file cannot be made | `E_IO` | `step` `lock`, `path` |
| The installer failed, or was stopped | `E_IO` | `step` `install`, `installer_exit` and `installer` (its last line), or `deadline_s` |
| A staged binary is not the release | `E_IO` | `step` `verify`, `expected`, `found` |
| A binary could not be renamed into place | `E_IO` | `step` `swap`, `path` |
| The receipt could not be read or written | `E_IO` | `step` `receipt`, `path` |

Exit 2 for `E_INVALID_ARG`, 4 for `E_BUSY` and `E_REMOTE_UNREACHABLE`, which can be run again,
and 1 for `E_IO`. Up to and including `verify`, nothing was replaced, and the message says so.
A `swap` that failed on `so` has replaced `swarmops`, and its message starts by saying so: run
`update` again.

### Automatic update's switch

`--status` reaches no network and says whether this install updates itself after a command.
`auto_update` is `on`, or the first of these that holds:

| `auto_update` | What decided |
| --- | --- |
| `off_source_build` | The build is no release's. |
| `off_no_receipt` | No receipt is beside the binaries. |
| `off` | The receipt says `auto_update = false`: `--auto off` wrote it, or the installer did (for `--no-auto-update`, a named `--version`, or root). |
| `off_env` | `SWARMOPS_AUTO_UPDATE` is `off`, or holds anything but `on` and `off`. Empty counts as unset. |
| `off_ci` | `CI` is set to anything but the empty string, `0` or `false`, and `SWARMOPS_AUTO_UPDATE` is not `on`. |
| `off_container` | `/.dockerenv` or `/run/.containerenv` exists, and `SWARMOPS_AUTO_UPDATE` is not `on`. |
| `off_owner` | The caller is root, or the install directory belongs to another user. |

`SWARMOPS_AUTO_UPDATE=on` only cancels the `CI` and container rules. No store, remote, workspace
file or MCP request reads or sets any of this.

`--auto off` and `--auto on` write the receipt's `auto_update`, through a temporary file renamed
over it, mode 0644, and reach no network. Keys this build does not know are kept; comments are
not. `--auto on` needs what `update` needs, so it never makes a receipt for a package's install;
`--auto off` where there is no receipt changes nothing and is no error. The result's
`auto_update` is the answer after the write: `--auto on` as root still says `off_owner`.

None of the rules stops an `update` you run yourself, which needs only a release's build and a
receipt.

`dir` is the install directory, there only when a receipt was found. `pending` is the note a
background run left: its `kind` (`updated`, `available` or
`failed`), the release it is about (`to`) and, for `updated`, the version replaced (`from`).
`--status` reads the note and leaves it.

### In the background

`update --background` does what automatic update does, in one run: a command starts it
([After a command](#after-a-command)), and it runs when you run it. Unless `auto_update` is `on`
it does nothing. Otherwise it takes the lock, waiting half a second at most (another update
running: nothing), and asks for the latest release as above. Where one of the two names is
missing or answers as another program, it stops there: it replaces no program whose version it
cannot tell. When the release is newer than what is installed, and no older than the program
that runs:

1. A release remembered as failed is left alone, until an `update` you run goes well.
2. One more HEAD request asks whether the release holds the file
   `auto-update-from-<major>.<minor>`, named for the minor line installed: the release's mark
   that a build of that line may install it unasked. GitHub sees the minor line in that address.
3. **302**, the redirect to a file the release holds: the release is installed as above, with
   three minutes for the installer. The note is `updated <from> <to>`. A release that was
   downloaded and refused, by the installer (a checksum that does not match, a host it has no
   build for) or because a staged binary is not the release, is remembered as failed at once,
   with the note `failed <to> <the installer's last line>`. One that could not be downloaded,
   was stopped at the three minutes, or could not be renamed into place may go well another
   day: the try is counted and nothing is said, the next day's check tries again, and the third
   try that fails is remembered as the failure, with its note.
4. **404**, no such file: the release is announced, not installed. The first time a release is
   seen unmarked, only that is remembered; the note `available <to>` is written the next time it
   is still unmarked, and once. A release is the latest before its marks are uploaded.
5. **Anything else**, or no answer: nothing is written, and the next run asks again.

It prints its envelope like every command, exit 0 unless the receipt is refused, with
`updated` and `pending` saying what it did; a request that fails changes nothing and is no
error. Only the latest release is ever looked at: an install on an older line installs nothing
automatically while the latest release carries no mark for that line.

### After a command

Where `auto_update` is `on`, every command that went well is followed by automatic update, once
its envelope is out. The command's envelope, exit code and `meta.elapsed_ms` are what they are
without it, and it waits for nothing.

1. **The note.** If the command's stderr is a terminal and a background run left a note, the
   command removes the note and prints it, one line on stderr after the envelope. Of several
   commands at once, one prints it. A command whose stderr is no terminal (a script, an agent's
   harness, `2>&1` into a pipe) prints nothing and leaves the note: `--status` gives it as
   `pending`.
2. **The check, once a day.** The lock file's modification time is when a check was last
   claimed. Less than 24 hours ago, the command is done. Otherwise it claims the check (it
   locks the file without waiting, looks at the time again, and sets it to now) and starts
   `update --background`. Of several commands at once, one claims it. The claim comes before
   any request, so a host without a network asks once a day and says nothing. A time in the
   future, as a clock set back leaves, counts as long ago.
3. **The run it starts** is this program again, detached: a process group of its own, `/` for
   its directory, no stdin, stdout or stderr, and without the descriptors 3 to 9 the command
   inherited (it is started through `/bin/sh`, which closes them), so that it does not hold a
   lock or a pipe of the caller's for as long as a download takes. A descriptor numbered 10 or
   more that the caller passed down without close-on-exec stays open in it. It has the command's
   environment.

The notes say what happened, and tell nobody to run anything:

```text
swarmops: updated from 0.12.0 to 0.13.0. Notes: https://github.com/KeiaiLab/SwarmOps/releases/tag/v0.13.0. Running mcp servers keep 0.12.0 until restarted.
swarmops: 0.13.0 is released and was not installed automatically. Notes: https://github.com/KeiaiLab/SwarmOps/releases/tag/v0.13.0.
swarmops: 0.13.0 could not be installed automatically: <the installer's last line>.
```

Their wording is no contract; `pending` is. A note is printed only where `auto_update` is `on`
for the command that would print it.

Automatic update follows no run that is not a command that went well: not `--help` or
`--version`, not a line that is refused, not a command that fails. And it follows none of
`mcp`, `serve`, `serve --prepare`, `auth git-credential`, `ws hook` and `update` itself: a host
that uses SwarmOps only through `swarmops mcp` never looks for a release and never prints a
note. A directory the caller cannot write is never claimed in, so nothing is started there.

### The files beside the binaries

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `.swarmops-receipt` | The installer's receipt: `receipt = 1` and `auto_update = true` or `false`. |
| `.swarmops-update.lock` | The lock, and what the background run remembers: a line each for the release last `seen` unmarked, `announced`, `tried` (with how many times) and `failed`. Its modification time is when a check was last claimed. |
| `.swarmops-update.note` | One line: the note a background run left, which `--status` gives as `pending`. |
| `.swarmops-update.d` | The staging directory, there only while an update runs; one left behind is removed by the next. |

The installer's `--uninstall` removes all four. See
[Install](../../guides/install.md) for the installer.

## Return information

`result` is a `UpdateOut` (`swarmops schema UpdateOut` prints its JSON Schema).

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `auto_update` | `AutoUpdate` | yes | Whether the install updates itself after a command, and if not, why. |
| `current` | `string` | yes | The installed version when the command ended. For the forms that ask no binary for its version (`--status`, `--auto`, a `--background` that stops before it looks), and where one of the two names has none, the running program's own. |
| `dir` | `string or null` | no | The directory the binaries are installed in, a path on the caller's host. Omitted when no receipt is beside them. |
| `latest` | `string or null` | no | The latest release. Omitted when the command did not look for it. |
| `notes` | `string or null` | no | The page of the latest release's notes. Omitted when the command did not look for it. |
| `pending` | `UpdatePending or null` | no | The note an automatic update left that no command has printed yet. Omitted when there is none. |
| `previous` | `string or null` | no | The version this run replaced. Omitted when nothing was replaced. |
| `updated` | `boolean` | yes | Whether this run replaced the program. False when the latest release is not newer than what is installed, and for the forms of the command that install nothing. |

Envelope `op`: `update`.

Exit codes:

- `0`: Success.
- `2`: The request or the command line is malformed.

## Errors

- [`E_INVALID_ARG`](../errors.md#e_invalid_arg) (exit 2): A malformed argument or request, including a command-line usage error.

Any command that opens a store may also fail with a store error, such as [`E_NOT_A_REPO`](../errors.md#e_not_a_repo), [`E_IO`](../errors.md#e_io) or [`E_STORE_CORRUPT`](../errors.md#e_store_corrupt); a command line the grammar refuses is [`E_INVALID_ARG`](../errors.md#e_invalid_arg) (exit 2).
